title: The Frog Crosses the Stones

concept.title: The cost of reaching a stone is the cheaper of the two ways it can be entered
body: A frog sits on the first of `n` stones in a row; the stone `i` has the height `h[i]`. From a stone it can jump to the **next** stone or to the stone **after the next**, and a jump from the stone `i` to the stone `j` costs `|h[i] - h[j]|` (the difference of the heights). What is the smallest total cost for the frog to reach the last stone? For the heights `10 30 40 20` the best plan is 10 -> 30 -> 20, for 20 + 10 = 30.

Let `cost(i)` be the smallest total cost to reach the stone `i`. The last jump came from the stone `i - 1` or from the stone `i - 2`, so **`cost(i) = min(cost(i - 1) + |h[i] - h[i-1]|, cost(i - 2) + |h[i] - h[i-2]|)`**. We start with `cost(0) = 0` and `cost(1) = |h[1] - h[0]|`, since the only way to the stone 1 is one jump. The answer is `cost(n - 1)`.

body.code:
a = 0                                 # cost(i - 2)
b = abs(h[1] - h[0])                  # cost(i - 1)
for i in range(2, n):
    a, b = b, min(b + abs(h[i] - h[i - 1]), a + abs(h[i] - h[i - 2]))
print(b)

body: This is the stairs problem where the price of a move depends on **both ends** of the move instead of the place it leaves. The recurrence is the same; only the price changes. The time is O(n) and the memory O(1); the total can reach about 2 * 10^14, so use 64-bit numbers.

statement: `n` stones stand in a row; the stone `i` has the height `h[i]`. A frog starts on the first stone and, in one jump, moves to the next stone or to the one after it. A jump from the stone `i` to the stone `j` costs `|h[i] - h[j]|`. Print the smallest total cost to reach the last stone.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of stones.
The second line has `n` numbers: the height of each stone, in order.
hints: Let cost(i) be the smallest cost to reach the stone i.
The last jump came from i - 1 or from i - 2; add the height difference of that jump.
